strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-hcttbjy5/call-0a5850f5ec0e45bb8e9c5e70880a616d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses the practically important problem of jointly selecting pipeline placement and DP/TP/FSDP strategies; a unified optimization view could be useful.

The evaluation uses measured training throughput across six model configurations and several distinct clusters, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge, rather than relying only on simulation. UniAP often matches or improves upon the available baselines, with a substantial 3.80x gain in the reported Llama-7B case.

The scalability experiment, restricted-space ablation, estimation-error analysis, and BERT case study provide useful evidence beyond the headline comparison and help interpret the hybrid strategies found by the planner.
The paper is generally organized clearly, with a workflow diagram, explicit constraints, a notation appendix, solver settings, and hardware/model descriptions.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. In Eq. (3), P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) expands into products of four binary variables, and Eq. (4) has the same issue; the max operator in Eq. (2) also needs an epigraph construction. No auxiliary-variable linearization or equivalent reformulation is supplied, so the stated model cannot directly justify the claimed Gurobi implementation or complexity.

The purported order-preserving constraints only make each stage's node set contiguous; they do not enforce monotonic stage order. For a two-node graph u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies Eqs. (6)-(8), while Eq. (4) charges no cross-stage communication. More generally, non-adjacent cross-stage edges are unmodeled. Thus, the documented feasible set contains invalid or incorrectly costed pipeline plans.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal solution is unsupported. The GPipe objective combines forward and backward bottlenecks using a stated 'high probability' assumption, the cost model is approximate, and Appendix E terminates Gurobi after 60 seconds or as early as a 4% MIP gap. Treating this fixed cutoff as constant time in Section 3.5 does not constitute a meaningful complexity analysis or an optimality guarantee.

Memory modeling is insufficiently specified and potentially inconsistent with GPipe: Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b=B/c to CostModeling, while GPipe can retain activations from multiple micro-batches, but no corresponding c factor appears in Eq. (5). This prevents verification that the optimizer's OOM-feasibility claims are correct.

The cost-model validation covers only the selected optimal strategies, whereas correct ranking over competing candidates is what planning requires. Figure 8 also plots negative values despite Eq. (13) defining an absolute, hence nonnegative, relative error. No rank correlation, worst-case error, or broad held-out candidate evaluation is reported.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed advantage of joint MIQP optimization. The ablation compares against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only spaces, not a matched hierarchical optimizer using the same candidates and cost model. Moreover, hierarchical optimization is not inherently suboptimal, contrary to the paper's unsupported blanket assertion.

Baseline and timing evidence is incomplete. Many Alpa entries are unavailable or fail, the DCU evaluation compares mainly with manual frameworks, and UniAP's reported optimization time explicitly measures UOP after profiling; analogous profiling or compilation accounting for baselines is unclear. The number of repetitions and meaning of the reported ± values are also unspecified.

Reproducibility is weak: no source code is provided, and essential details such as construction of the strategy dictionary, resharding matrices, overlap coefficients, profiling protocol, execution-plan translation, software versions, and baseline tuning are omitted. Dependence on a commercial Gurobi solver adds another barrier.

The contribution is primarily a distributed-training systems optimizer. Only two evaluated models are vision models, and there is no vision-specific methodology or accuracy/convergence study, leaving its direct contribution to computer vision relatively limited.

strengths: The work addresses an important practical problem: jointly selecting pipeline, data, tensor, and fully sharded parallelism could substantially reduce expert tuning effort.

The evaluation spans six Transformer models, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge, and diverse hardware from 8 to 64 accelerators. UniAP often matches the strongest baseline and reports meaningful gains on EnvB and a 3.80× Llama-7B gain on EnvC.

The restricted-space ablation supports the usefulness of combining inter- and intra-layer choices. The scalability study, cost-estimation analysis, notation table, solver settings, and strategy visualization are also valuable.
The manuscript is generally well organized and explains the intended cost model and optimization workflow clearly.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. Equations (3) and (4) contain degree-four products such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v), while Equation (2) contains a max operator. No auxiliary variables or equivalent linear/quadratic reformulation are provided, so the stated program cannot directly be implemented by the claimed solver formulation.

The constraints do not enforce topological ordering of pipeline stages. For an edge u→v, placing u in stage 2 and v in stage 1 satisfies the per-stage contiguity constraints when both stages are singletons. Equation (4), which charges only transitions from stage j to j+1, then omits this communication entirely. Edges that skip stages are likewise unaddressed. This can produce invalid or systematically under-costed solutions.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal strategy is unsupported. The search excludes non-factor pipeline and microbatch counts, uses a 60-second solver limit, and may terminate at a 4% MIP gap. Moreover, the GPipe latency expression is an approximation and cost estimates have nonzero error. No solver gaps or exhaustive small-instance comparison establishes global optimality. Treating the bounded solver call as constant time also makes the stated polynomial complexity a runtime-cap analysis rather than the complexity of solving the NP-hard program.

The peak-memory model is internally unclear: Algorithm 1 constructs M using microbatch size b=B/c, but Equation (5) has no dependence on c even though GPipe retains activations from multiple microbatches before backward execution. Without a schedule-aware peak-memory derivation or validation, feasibility and OOM avoidance are not technically established.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP/TP/FSDP strategies. Casting these interacting decisions into one optimization framework is potentially useful.

The empirical study spans several model families and four substantially different hardware environments. UniAP achieves meaningful measured gains in some settings, including 1.20–1.71× on BERT-Huge, 1.18–1.41× on ViT-Huge, 1.37× on Swin-Huge, and 3.80× on one Llama-7B configuration.
The manuscript provides an algorithm, notation table, cost-model evaluation, ablations, and a concrete BERT-Huge strategy case study. These make the intended workflow reasonably clear.
Reporting throughput variation and optimization time is valuable, and the average 3.59% estimation error on the evaluated selected strategies is encouraging.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. Equations (3) and (4) contain products such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v), which are fourth-degree terms, while Equation (2) contains a max operator. No auxiliary-variable reformulation, linearization, or equivalence proof is supplied. Consequently, the stated optimization cannot be reproduced or verified from the manuscript.

The placement constraints appear incomplete. Contiguity of each stage does not enforce that edges follow increasing pipeline-stage order or connect allowable consecutive stages. Reversed or stage-skipping assignments can therefore satisfy the presented constraints, while Equation (4) charges only edges from stage j to j+1. Such assignments may be invalid yet artificially inexpensive.

Repeated claims of finding an optimal solution are unsupported. Gurobi is stopped after 60 seconds and may terminate after 15 seconds with a 4% optimality gap; optimization is also over a predefined strategy dictionary using an approximate cost model. The complexity analysis further hides the NP-hard solver cost by treating the timeout as a constant. At most, the reported procedure returns a bounded-time approximate solution in a restricted modeled space.

The GPipe model needs stronger justification. Equation (2) merges forward and backward bottlenecks based only on a 'high probability' ordering assumption. More seriously, Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size B/c into the memory model, although GPipe ordinarily retains activations across its micro-batches before backward propagation and activation checkpointing is disabled. The manuscript does not explain where this c-dependent activation memory is accounted for.

The evidence does not establish that joint MIQP optimization, rather than implementation or search-budget differences, causes the gains. The ablation compares against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only spaces, not hierarchical joint optimization. Gurobi uses multiple threads while competing planners are described as single-threaded, and profiling time is excluded without an end-to-end overhead comparison.

Baseline coverage is uneven: Alpa is unavailable, fails, or exceeds the cutoff in most rows; Galvatron matches UniAP on three ENVA models and slightly exceeds it on ENVB T5; and the DCU experiments show equal throughput to Megatron. The headline 3.80× throughput gain comes from one model/environment comparison.

Cost-model validation covers only the strategies selected by UniAP, rather than representative candidate strategies or ranking accuracy. Thus, low average prediction error does not demonstrate that the predicted optimum is the fastest feasible execution plan, especially when individual errors approach 10%.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code, detailed strategy-dictionary construction, complete profiling methodology and overhead, software versions, and sufficiently detailed baseline configuration. Reliance on proprietary Gurobi also raises an additional reproducibility barrier.

The novelty claim relative to Piper, Alpa, and other multidimensional planners is asserted mainly by labeling their searches hierarchical; the paper provides neither a formal search-space comparison nor evidence that hierarchy necessarily makes their solutions suboptimal. CVPR relevance is also indirect: the contribution is a generic distributed-systems planner, with vision evidence limited to throughput on ViT and Swin.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: automatically combining pipeline placement with per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP choices could substantially reduce expert tuning and is potentially useful for large-model training.

The measured performance signal is meaningful. On ENVB-8, UniAP improves over the strongest reported baseline by approximately 20% for BERT-Huge, 18% for ViT-Huge, and 37% for Swin-Huge; it reports a 3.80x gain over Galvatron for Llama-7B on ENVC and matches Galvatron on three ENVA models.

The evaluation covers diverse hardware—V100, TITAN Xp, A100, and non-NVIDIA DCUs—and six model configurations spanning vision and language. The cost-model study, scalability experiments, ablation, and concrete BERT strategy visualization are useful additions.

The manuscript is generally well organized, and the diagrams make the intended search space and resulting hybrid strategies understandable. Hardware, batch-size, model, and Gurobi configurations are partially documented. The complete manuscript was inspected: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-bv1btmmv/call-c6f1f963515e4b278ed37a8da964e3df/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: Equations (3) and (4) are not MIQP constraints as written because P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R S_v) contains products of four binary variables; no auxiliary-variable reformulation is provided. The max operator in Equation (2) is likewise not reformulated. More seriously, the constraints do not require stage indices to follow graph order: for an edge u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 can satisfy the contiguity constraints, while Equation (4) charges no cross-stage communication. Thus the stated program can produce invalid or artificially cheap solutions.

The repeated global-optimality claim is unsupported. Appendix E permits termination after 15 seconds with a 4% MIP gap and imposes a 60-second limit, while the objective itself is estimated. The search is also restricted to divisor-valued pipeline and micro-batch counts; notably, the paper describes Galvatron using three micro-batches for batch size eight, a configuration UniAP's enumeration excludes. Treating the time-limited NP-hard MIQP solver as constant time also makes the claimed polynomial complexity misleading.

The GPipe cost and memory models need stronger justification. Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size B/c to the memory model, but Equation (5) has no factor accounting for the c forward activations retained by checkpoint-free GPipe. Equation (2) combines forward and backward bottlenecks using only a 'high probability' argument. No memory-prediction or candidate-ranking validation is supplied. Additionally, Figure 8 displays negative errors although Equation (13) defines an absolute, nonnegative error.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the benefit of joint rather than hierarchical optimization. Figure 6 compares the full method only against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only restrictions, not a hierarchical search implemented with the same execution engine and cost model. Alpa uses a different framework, ENVD has only manual baselines, and several headline comparisons rely on baseline failures or unavailable implementations. The reported planning time measures UOP only, excluding UniAP's profiling overhead, and contrasts multithreaded Gurobi with serial baseline searches.

Validation is limited to throughput over iterations 10–60. There are no loss curves, final task accuracies, or numerical-equivalence checks showing that the generated TP/FSDP execution plans preserve training behavior. The number of independent runs and statistical procedure are unspecified. The main scalability experiment increases batch size with device count, so it demonstrates weak scaling rather than strong-scaling efficiency.

The contribution is primarily a general ML-systems planner rather than a computer-vision or pattern-recognition method. ViT and Swin provide some CV relevance, but there is no vision-specific insight or end-to-end visual-task accuracy evaluation. Moreover, the 'first joint method' claim is asserted rather than established through a precise search-space comparison with Alpa, Piper, and Galvatron.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a systems contribution: no code or artifact is identified, and essential details are missing for the strategy dictionary, polynomial reformulation, topology/device-group selection, profiling workloads, overlap-coefficient estimation, execution-plan generation, software versions, baseline tuning, and achieved solver gaps. Minor notation inconsistencies and language errors are secondary presentation issues and do not determine the score; the rejection direction is driven by the formulation and evidence gaps above.

strengths: Jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies is well motivated and could substantially reduce expert tuning effort.

The evaluation covers five Transformer families and four substantially different hardware environments, including multi-node NVIDIA and DCU clusters. UniAP is competitive in most reported settings and achieves meaningful gains, including 3.80× throughput over Galvatron for Llama-7B on ENVC.
The paper includes useful scalability experiments, a comparison of restricted strategy spaces, cost-estimation results, and a concrete case study explaining the selected BERT-Huge strategy.
The manuscript is generally clear and supplements the main presentation with notation, a contiguity proof, solver settings, and model and hardware details.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. In Eq. (3), P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) is quartic in decision variables, as is the corresponding term in Eq. (4); even the remaining equalities contain quadratic constraints. The manuscript gives no auxiliary-variable reformulation or linearization that Gurobi 10.1 could solve as the claimed MIQP, leaving a consequential gap between the mathematical method and implementation.

The placement constraints do not require stage indices to follow graph order or require every cross-stage edge to join consecutive stages. Eq. (4) charges only edges directed from stage j to j+1, so reversed or skipped stage assignments can have uncounted communication costs under the stated model.

Claims of finding an optimal strategy are unsupported. Runs stop after 60 seconds and may stop after 15 seconds with a relative MIP gap below 4%, yet final gaps and solver statuses are not reported. Optimization also uses an approximate cost model. Treating solver time as a constant in Section 3.5 therefore neither establishes the stated polynomial complexity nor preserves exact optimality.

The GPipe cost and memory models need stronger justification. Eq. (2) replaces separate forward and backward bottlenecks with max_i(fp_i+bp_i), which is exact only under additional bottleneck assumptions. Moreover, Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b=B/c to the memory model even though checkpoint-free GPipe retains activations from multiple in-flight micro-batches; the formulation shows no factor accounting for this accumulation.

The claimed global optimum and “largest strategy space” apply only to a restricted, insufficiently characterized dictionary: pipeline degree and micro-batch count must divide GPU count and batch size, stage device counts are uniform, and the demonstrated schedule is GPipe. Nonuniform allocations, activation checkpointing, alternative schedules, and heterogeneous clusters are excluded.

The evidence does not establish actual-strategy optimality. Cost error is measured only on selected strategies rather than over candidate rankings, and no manageable case is exhaustively executed to verify that the predicted optimum is fastest. The headline 3.80× result compares against only Galvatron in one Llama setting; Alpa is unavailable for several cases, while the DCU experiments tie Megatron's best throughput and compare optimization procedures with substantially different costs.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code and insufficient specification of the strategy dictionary, graph construction, resharding matrices, profiling protocol, and runtime integration. Reproduction also depends on a commercial solver.

The contribution is primarily generic distributed-training systems work. Only ViT and Swin among the evaluated families are vision models, and there is no vision-specific methodological or empirical finding, making the fit and direct contribution to CVPR comparatively limited.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies. A topology-aware unified planner could substantially reduce expert tuning effort.

The evaluation uses real training runs across four hardware environments and six model variants, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge. UniAP is competitive or best in most reported comparisons, with meaningful gains on ENVB-8 and a 3.80× gain for Llama-7B on ENVC.

The ablation indicates that combining inter- and intra-layer choices can improve feasibility and throughput over either restricted search space. The scalability experiments, cost-estimation study, and BERT case study add useful complementary evidence.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly, and the appendix provides notation, solver settings, model configurations, and an interpretable example strategy.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. Equations (3) and (4) multiply two placement variables by the quadratic term S_u^T R S_v, producing fourth-degree expressions; Equation (5) is also bilinear, and the max in Equation (2) is not reformulated. No auxiliary-variable linearization is given, so the stated formulation cannot directly support the claimed Gurobi MIQP implementation.

The placement constraints do not enforce pipeline-stage precedence. For a two-node edge u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies the stated contiguity and assignment constraints, while Equation (4) charges no cross-stage communication. Nonconsecutive cross-stage edges are likewise unmodeled. This is a consequential correctness issue because the optimizer can admit invalid or artificially inexpensive plans.

Claims of finding an optimal strategy are unsupported. The solver stops after 60 seconds or at a relative gap below 4%, costs are estimated, and the search restricts stage counts and micro-batch counts to selected factors and apparently assumes equal device allocations and uniform micro-batches. The complexity analysis treats capped solver time as constant, thereby avoiding rather than analyzing the exponential optimization cost and its loss of optimality.

The described GPipe memory model appears to underestimate activation storage: Algorithm 1 constructs memory costs using micro-batch size b=B/c, although GPipe without activation checkpointing retains activations from multiple forward micro-batches until backward execution. The paper neither includes the corresponding factor nor experimentally validates peak-memory predictions.

The evidence does not establish reliable strategy ranking. Figure 8 evaluates only a small number of selected solutions rather than the candidate space, provides no small-instance oracle comparison, and plots negative errors despite Equation (13) defining an absolute nonnegative error. Solver gaps, timeout frequency, and feasibility-prediction accuracy are not reported.

The optimization-time comparison is confounded by multi-threaded Gurobi versus single-threaded baselines, different frameworks, numerous OOM or unavailable baseline entries, and exclusion of profiling and compilation costs. The headline 3.80× throughput gain comes from one Llama comparison; the two vision-model comparisons are substantially more modest.

Reproducibility and CVPR relevance are limited. No code availability is stated, and important details such as the exact strategy dictionary, polynomial linearization, resharding-cost construction, overlap model, software versions, profiling overhead, and error-bar protocol are missing. The vision evaluation covers only ImageNet classification with two Transformer models, without a broader vision task or CV-specific insight.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-q0y540ty/call-b538517590cd4b8aafd4900e67a757f6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important systems problem. Jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies is practically useful and more expressive than separate searches.

The evaluation uses actual training runs across four hardware environments, six model configurations, and up to 64 accelerators. UniAP matches Galvatron on three ENVA models, improves over the strongest available baseline by 18-37% on three ENVB workloads, and reports a 3.80x Llama-7B gain over Galvatron on ENVC.
The inter-only/intra-only ablation, topology-aware BERT case study, and reported 3.59% average throughput-estimation error provide useful evidence that combining strategy classes can matter.
The paper is clearly organized and visually polished. Hardware, batch sizes, model configurations, solver settings, and the principal formulation are documented in substantial detail.
weaknesses: Material correctness issue: the formulation is not an MIQP as written. Terms such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) in Equations (3) and (4) expand to products of four binary variables. No auxiliary-variable reformulation or linearization is given, so an MIQP solver cannot directly solve the stated program.

Material correctness issue: the contiguity constraints do not enforce monotonic pipeline-stage order. Contiguous layer blocks can be assigned reversed stage labels while satisfying Equation (6), whereas Equation (4) charges only edges from stage j to j+1; reversed or nonconsecutive cross-stage edges can therefore be omitted from the modeled cost.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal solution is contradicted by the implementation: Gurobi may stop at a 4% gap after 15 seconds or at a 60-second limit, and achieved gaps are not reported. The search also restricts pipeline sizes and micro-batch counts to divisors, while the complexity analysis treats the capped NP-hard MIQP solve as constant time.

The documented GPipe memory model appears incomplete. Algorithm 1 computes activation memory using micro-batch size b=B/c, but the illustrated flush schedule retains activations for c forward micro-batches and activation checkpointing is disabled; no corresponding factor is described. Moreover, Figure 8 shows negative values despite Equation (13) defining a nonnegative absolute error.

The experimental evidence is narrower than the broad universality claims: direct AP comparisons are mostly on eight accelerators; Alpa is unavailable for several cases; ENVB uses a reduced 16/16-layer T5; and the 32-64 accelerator experiments compare only manual baselines. The scaling experiments increase batch size with device count, demonstrating weak scaling rather than fixed-workload scaling.

Reproducibility remains limited because no code is provided, and key details such as the strategy dictionary, formulation linearization, number of independent runs, and profiling overhead are absent. Optimization-time comparisons exclude profiling and mix Gurobi's multithreaded search with different baseline implementations. The contribution is also primarily distributed-ML systems work, with only two vision architectures used as workloads.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-w4og1bzd/call-b949151279d042d4899e7cf9c19f0053/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important systems problem: jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP/TP/FSDP strategies. This is more ambitious than optimizing either category alone or using a fixed hierarchical decomposition.

The evaluation is unusually broad in hardware, covering V100, TITAN Xp, A100, and non-NVIDIA DCU clusters, including multinode experiments up to 64 devices. It also includes six sizable Transformer models, two of which are vision architectures.

Several measured gains are practically significant: UniAP improves throughput by 1.18–1.71× on three ENVB-8 cases and by 3.80× for Llama-7B on ENVC, while finding feasible configurations in cases where baselines fail. The BERT case study gives an intuitive explanation of the resulting hybrid strategy.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with an explicit optimization objective, algorithm, notation table, cost-model study, restricted-search ablation, and interpretable strategy visualizations.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: Equations (3) and (4) are not MIQP constraints as written. The term P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) contains products of four binary variables, while the max in Equation (2) also requires an unreported epigraph or general-constraint transformation. No auxiliary-variable linearization is supplied, so the stated formulation cannot directly be reproduced with the specified Gurobi 10.1 solver.

Material technical issue: the constraints do not enforce that pipeline-stage indices follow graph order. For a two-node chain u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies the stated contiguity and placement constraints, but Equation (4), which only counts edges from stage j to j+1, charges no cross-stage communication. Edges that skip stages are likewise unmodeled. Consequently, the written program can favor incorrectly costed placements.

Material claim mismatch: the repeated claim of finding an optimal solution is unsupported. Each solve has a 60-second limit and may stop after 15 seconds with a 4% MIP gap; the cost model is approximate as well. No achieved gaps, optimality certificates, or exhaustive small-instance comparisons are reported. Treating solver time as a constant in the complexity analysis also obscures the NP-hard optimization rather than characterizing it.

The evidence does not isolate the claimed advantage over hierarchical optimization. Figure 6 compares the full space only with inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only restrictions; improvement from a superset is expected and does not compare against a controlled hierarchical planner using the same cost model, implementation, and strategy space. The strongest baselines are largely from 2022, weakening the 2025 state-of-the-art claim.

The cost-model validation is internally inconsistent: Equation (13) defines a nonnegative absolute relative error, whereas Figure 8 plots negative values. Moreover, it evaluates only approximately eight selected strategies, not prediction quality or ranking regret over the candidate space, which is what determines whether the chosen strategy is actually best.

Reproducibility is limited despite some useful configuration details. There is no code or execution artifact, and the exact strategy dictionary, profiling procedure and cost, software versions, device-group construction, number of independent runs, and meaning of the reported ± values are missing. Dependence on a commercial Gurobi solver further raises the replication barrier.

For CVPR, the contribution is primarily general ML systems research: four of six models are NLP models, and the vision evidence is limited to throughput on ViT and Swin without a vision-specific methodological contribution or end-to-end training validation. Together with the formulation and optimality problems, this makes the current balance a weak reject rather than a borderline acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript presents a useful systems idea: jointly selecting PP, DP, TP, and FSDP strategies instead of optimizing inter- and intra-layer parallelism hierarchically. The unified optimization perspective is potentially valuable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-iu3bzl0g/call-fda2c81a9b5f4a4d937fca548d45d4b2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation has meaningful breadth: multiple single- and multi-node environments using V100, TITAN Xp, A100, and DCU accelerators; six model configurations; and both vision and language Transformers.

The reported empirical gains are sometimes substantial. On ENVB-8, UniAP improves ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge throughput by 18–41% over available baselines, and the Llama-7B result on ENVC is 3.80× faster than Galvatron. The paper also reports cases where methods tie or UniAP is slightly worse, rather than presenting only wins.

The manuscript is generally organized well and includes hardware/model configurations, solver settings, a cost-estimation study, a restricted-search ablation, and an interpretable case study of the selected BERT strategy.
weaknesses: The central mathematical formulation is not an MIQP as written. In Eq. (3), P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) is fourth degree in binary variables, as is the corresponding term in Eq. (4). Even an MIQCP permits only quadratic expressions. No auxiliary variables or linearization constraints are supplied, so the stated formulation cannot directly be given to Gurobi and the implemented optimization problem is not reproducible from the paper.

The placement constraints admit invalid or under-costed pipelines. Equations (6) enforce that each stage's node set is contiguous but do not enforce monotonic stage indices along graph edges. For a two-node chain u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 satisfies Eqs. (6)–(8), yet Eq. (4) charges no cross-stage communication. Edges that skip stage indices are likewise unmodeled. This can change the optimizer's solution, not merely its presentation.

The repeated claim of finding an “optimal solution” is unsupported. Appendix E terminates Gurobi after 15 seconds with a MIP gap below 4% and imposes a 60-second limit, while the objective itself uses an approximate cost model. The stated polynomial complexity also excludes the NP-hard optimization by treating this timeout as constant; exact optimality and the complexity argument cannot both hold.

The GPipe memory accounting appears inconsistent with its fill-drain schedule. Section 3.2 scales activation memory by batch size, while Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b=B/c to the cost model. Without activation checkpointing, which the experiments explicitly disable, GPipe retains activations for all c forward micro-batches before backward execution. Unless an unreported factor of c is included, Eq. (5) can substantially underestimate peak memory and admit OOM strategies.

Evidence that the estimated optimum is the fastest realizable strategy is limited. Figure 8 evaluates only the selected strategies from ENVA and ENVB—approximately eight points—and reports mean prediction error, but provides neither ranking accuracy over candidate strategies nor exhaustive optimality checks on tractable configurations. Low error on already-selected points does not establish reliable strategy ordering.

Several headline comparisons are weakly supported. UniAP ties Galvatron on three ENVA models and is slightly slower on T5-Large on ENVB-8; Alpa is unavailable or fails for several settings. The ENVD comparison measures cost-model planning against hours of manual Megatron enumeration, while DeepSpeed is configured with a batch size that cannot launch, making Table 2 less informative as a state-of-the-art comparison.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript provides no code artifact, full strategy dictionary, explicit construction of the cost matrices and overlap coefficients, or independent-run protocol. Reported deviations appear to come from iterations 10–60, but the number of independent trials is unspecified, and profiling time is excluded from the optimization-time metric. These limitations compound the central formulation errors, so the current balance favors rejection despite the promising idea and empirical results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: jointly selecting pipeline, data, tensor, and fully sharded data parallelism could substantially reduce expert effort in large-model training.

The proposed integration of stage placement and intra-layer strategies is conceptually useful. The manuscript considers computation, communication, resharding, memory, topology, and overlap costs, and supplements the method with notation, a contiguity proof, and an interpretable case study.

The evaluation covers multiple accelerator types, single- and multi-node environments, NLP models, and two vision architectures. UniAP reports meaningful gains on ENVB-8 and a 3.80x gain for Llama-7B on ENVC; the strategy-space ablation and reported 3.59% mean estimation error provide additional supporting evidence.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with readable figures and tables. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-qf26kbwn/call-6ecab63cc4494eec9c0679294a72354c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. In Equations (3) and (4), P_ui P_vi multiplies S_u^T R_uv S_v, producing degree-four terms; Equation (2) also contains an unformulated max operator. No joint variables, auxiliary constraints, or other transformation reducing these expressions to quadratic form is provided, so the claimed optimization problem and implementation cannot be verified.

The placement constraints do not enforce forward ordering of numbered pipeline stages or account for arbitrary cross-stage edges. For a simple edge u→v, assigning u to stage 2 and v to stage 1 can satisfy the stated contiguity constraints, while Equation (4), which charges only stage j→j+1 edges, omits its communication. This materially questions feasibility and cost correctness.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal strategy is unsupported. Gurobi is stopped after 60 seconds and may terminate after a reported gap below 4%; the planner also restricts stage counts and micro-batch counts to divisors, appears to use equal-width stages, and primarily models GPipe. Moreover, a 3.59% approximate cost-model error can alter the ranking of close candidates. The evidence therefore supports a useful heuristic planner, not exact global optimality.

The GPipe memory model is insufficiently specified and appears inconsistent: Algorithm 1 builds costs using micro-batch size b=B/c, but Equation (5) contains no factor accounting for the c sets of activations retained by a GPipe schedule. Cost accuracy is evaluated only on a small set of selected strategies, rather than across candidates with ranking and OOM-prediction accuracy, so feasibility reliability is not established.

The comparison does not fully substantiate the headline generality. Several entries tie or slightly trail Galvatron, Alpa is unavailable or fails on multiple cases, and the 3.80x throughput gain comes from one Llama configuration. Search-time comparisons are confounded by multithreaded commercial Gurobi versus serial or failed baselines, while profiling overhead is excluded. The scaling experiments also increase batch size with device count and thus demonstrate weak rather than strong scaling.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of released implementation details, the complete strategy dictionary, profiling workload and overhead, software versions, independent-run counts, and per-instance solver gaps or bounds. The contribution is also primarily a generic distributed-systems planner; evidence of impact on computer vision is limited to throughput measurements on ViT and Swin. These issues are secondary to, but compound, the central formulation problems.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: jointly selecting pipeline, data, tensor, and fully sharded data parallelism could reduce substantial manual engineering effort.
The profiler-to-cost-model-to-optimizer workflow is understandable, and Algorithm 1, the notation appendix, and the BERT-Huge topology case study make the high-level approach relatively accessible.

The evaluation covers five model families, six model configurations, four hardware environments, and clusters of 8–64 accelerators. It includes throughput, planning time, scalability, an ablation, estimation error, and variability measurements.

Some empirical improvements are substantial: on ENVB-8, UniAP improves BERT-Huge, ViT-Huge, and Swin-Huge throughput, while on ENVC it obtains 4.63 versus 1.22 samples/s for Llama-7B against Galvatron. These results indicate potential systems usefulness.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: the optimization problem is not an MIQP as written. In Eq. 3, P_ui P_vi multiplied by S_u^T R_uv S_v is fourth degree in binary variables; Eq. 4 has the same problem, and Eq. 2 contains an unmodeled maximum. No auxiliary variables or equivalent reduction to quadratic form is given, so the stated formulation cannot be reproduced or verified as the claimed Gurobi MIQP.

Material correctness issue: Constraints 6a–6c enforce contiguity but do not enforce monotonic pipeline-stage indices. Even for a chain, later layers may be assigned to stage 1 and earlier layers to stage 2 while satisfying the constraints. Equation 4 also charges only edges directed from stage j to j+1, omitting reversed assignments and edges crossing nonconsecutive stages. Thus the written program admits invalid or under-costed placements.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal solution is unsupported. The planner restricts stage counts and micro-batch counts to factors of n and B, assumes equal-sized stage device groups, and uses a GPipe-specific schedule and a preconstructed strategy dictionary. Moreover, Gurobi is stopped after 60 seconds or at an early-stopping gap as large as 4%, while costs are estimated rather than exact. No achieved gaps or optimality certificates are reported.

The complexity analysis is misleading: treating a fixed solver timeout as constant does not make an NP-hard MIQP solver an O(1) operation or preserve optimality. Constructing pairwise resharding terms also generally depends on |E||S|², which is absent from the claimed O(|V||S|sqrt(Bn)) bound.

The memory model is insufficiently justified for the illustrated GPipe schedule. Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b=B/c to cost modeling, while Eq. 5 contains no factor for the c simultaneously retained activation sets or a tensor-liveness analysis. Figure 6 additionally reports that a UniAP restricted variant returns a placement that encounters CUDA OOM, showing that the constraint does not consistently guarantee feasibility.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the central contribution. UniAP, Galvatron, and Alpa use different frameworks and available operator support; Alpa is unavailable, fails compilation, exceeds 40 minutes, or runs out of memory in many rows. The 3.80× headline comes from one Llama comparison, whereas several other results tie and T5-Large on ENVB-8 is slightly worse. Figure 6 compares joint search only with inter-only and intra-only search, not with a hierarchical inter-plus-intra planner under the same runtime and cost model.

Reproducibility is weak: there is no implementation link, the strategy dictionary and execution-plan translation are underspecified, profiling overhead is excluded from the reported UOP time, software versions and independent trial counts are absent, and the method depends on commercial Gurobi plus platform-specific DCU libraries. No loss-equivalence or convergence check verifies that complex combined strategies preserve training semantics.

The contribution is only indirectly connected to computer vision: it is a general distributed-training systems paper, with ViT and Swin used merely as two throughput workloads and no vision-specific method, recognition result, or scientific insight. This is a significant CVPR-fit concern. Minor typos and terminology inconsistencies are secondary and do not drive the recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies. A genuinely unified, topology-aware optimizer would reduce substantial expert effort and be useful for training large vision and language models. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-pz7euj93/call-32b215d34376447eb2f0f082ad680480/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The experiments cover several hardware regimes and six model configurations, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge. UniAP obtains meaningful gains in some settings, such as 45.58 versus 38.74 samples/s for ViT-Huge on EnvB-8 and 4.63 versus 1.22 for Llama-7B on EnvC.

The reported strategy-search times are consistently favorable, and the scaling experiments reach 64 accelerators. The BERT case study also provides useful qualitative evidence that combining PP, DP, TP, and FSDP can exploit hierarchical interconnects.
The high-level workflow, notation table, hardware descriptions, batch sizes, solver settings, and throughput measurement interval are presented clearly.
weaknesses: Material—core formulation correctness: Equations (3) and (4) are not MIQP constraints as written. Terms such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) multiply four binary decision variables and are quartic, while the max term in Equation (2) is also not reformulated. No auxiliary-variable linearization is supplied, and Gurobi 10.1 cannot directly treat these expressions as an MIQP. Thus the central claimed formulation cannot be reproduced or verified from the manuscript.

Material—invalid stage assignments remain feasible. Constraints (6)-(8) make each stage's node set contiguous but do not enforce topological ordering of stage indices or require crossing edges to join consecutive stages. For a simple chain, assigning earlier layers to stage 2 and later layers to stage 1 satisfies contiguity, while Equation (4) counts only stage j to j+1 edges and therefore omits the crossing communication. This can produce an invalid or artificially cheap optimizer solution.

Material—the repeated claim of finding an optimal strategy is unsupported. The solver has a 60-second limit and can stop after 15 seconds at a relative gap below 4%, yet final gaps or optimality certificates are not reported. Moreover, the objective uses an approximate cost model and a predefined candidate dictionary. The stated polynomial complexity also hides the NP-hard MIQP solve by treating its time limit as a constant; bounded runtime is not complexity for obtaining an optimum.

Material—the described GPipe memory accounting appears inconsistent. Algorithm 1 constructs costs using micro-batch size b=B/c, and activation memory is defined as batch size times per-sample memory. With checkpointing explicitly disabled, GPipe retains activations for all c forward micro-batches until backward execution, so Equation (5) does not clearly account for peak activation memory or establish its claimed OOM guarantee.

The evidence for the cost model is too narrow to rescue these correctness concerns. Figure 8 evaluates only eight selected solutions, not ranking accuracy across candidate strategies; it also plots negative errors although Equation (13) defines a nonnegative absolute relative error. The claimed 3.59% average is consequently ambiguous.

The empirical advantage is uneven. UniAP ties Galvatron on three EnvA models, is slightly worse on EnvB T5, and ties manual Megatron throughput on both EnvD Llama models. The 3.80× headline gain comes from one model/hardware comparison; Alpa is unavailable or fails in several rows. In Figure 6, joint search improves over the better restricted variant clearly only for T5, while tying one restricted variant for BERT, ViT, and Swin.

Material—reproducibility is insufficient: the manuscript gives no code link and does not specify construction of the strategy dictionary, reformulation sent to Gurobi, resharding matrices, CCOC estimation, or translation into executable plans. Search-time comparisons measure UOP while omitting the upfront profiling cost, without demonstrating equivalent accounting for baselines. These omissions concern the core method rather than presentation polish.

Presentation/scope refinements are secondary: the claim that MFU is independent of hardware and implementation is incorrect, independent-run counts are not given, and computer-vision validation is limited to two Transformer classifiers. These alone would not determine rejection, but the formulation and optimality problems do.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a potentially useful unified planner that selects pipeline placement together with per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies while considering topology, resharding, communication overlap, and memory.

The evaluation is reasonably broad, covering four hardware environments, up to 64 accelerators, and both vision and language Transformers. Reported gains include 1.41x on ViT-Huge, 1.37x on Swin-Huge, and 3.80x on Llama-7B over Galvatron in the corresponding settings.

The restricted-search-space ablation supports the qualitative motivation that combining inter- and intra-layer choices can find strategies unavailable to either category alone. The weak-scaling experiments and cost-estimation comparison provide additional useful evidence.
The manuscript is generally well organized. The flowchart, notation appendix, topology case study, and explicit cost components make the intended approach understandable.
weaknesses: The central mathematical formulation is not an MIQP as written. In Equations (3) and (4), P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) expands into products of four binary variables. No combined variables or linearization constraints are introduced, so the displayed program cannot directly be handled as the claimed quadratic program.

The stage constraints are incorrect for the stated purpose. Equations (6a)-(6c) make each stage's node set contiguous but do not enforce topological ordering of stage indices. For a chain, assigning an early contiguous block to stage 2 and a later block to stage 1 remains feasible, while Equation (4) counts only edges from stage j to j+1 and therefore omits that boundary's communication. General DAG edges that skip stages are likewise unmodeled.

The GPipe memory guarantee appears invalid. Algorithm 1 builds M using micro-batch size b=B/c, but fill-drain GPipe retains activations from all c forward micro-batches until their backward passes. Equation (5) contains no corresponding factor c, despite activation checkpointing being disabled, and can therefore substantially underestimate memory and return infeasible strategies.

The claim of finding an optimal solution is not supported. The cost model and GPipe objective are approximations; the search assumes factorized, apparently equal-width stage allocations; and the appendix imposes a 60-second solver limit with early termination at a 4% MIP gap. No achieved gaps or optimality certificates are reported. Treating the solver time limit as a constant also does not constitute a complexity analysis of exact MIQP optimization.

Equation (2) is not generally the exact GPipe makespan: forward and backward phases can have different bottleneck stages or communication links, whereas it uses the maximum of combined forward-plus-backward costs. The manuscript justifies this through a heuristic correlation, further weakening the global-optimality claim.

The evidence does not verify that cost minimization reliably selects the fastest real strategy. The 3.59% estimation error is reported only for selected strategies, without candidate-wide error, ranking correlation, or comparison to an exhaustive oracle on tractable cases. The ablation also does not compare against a hierarchical planner under an identical search space and execution stack.

The largest planning-time comparison excludes profiling, contrasts multithreaded Gurobi with reportedly single-threaded baselines, and does not control or report planning compute resources. Several baseline entries are censored, unavailable, out of memory, or return no solution, making the headline 107x and some practical comparisons difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of released code and insufficient specification of the strategy dictionary, device-group enumeration, profiling procedure, repetition counts, and meaning of the error bars. Dependence on proprietary Gurobi adds another barrier. The contribution is also primarily a distributed-systems optimization method, with only two vision-model evaluations and limited direct computer-vision insight.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a conceptually appealing joint search over pipeline, data, tensor, and fully sharded parallelism instead of a hierarchical search.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering several GPU/DCU environments and six Transformer configurations, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge. Measured throughput improvements reach 3.80×, and the planner is often substantially faster than the evaluated automatic-parallelism baselines.

The topology-aware profiling, restricted-search ablation, scaling experiments, and BERT-Huge strategy case study provide useful evidence that jointly selecting inter- and intra-layer strategies can improve practical training performance.
The manuscript is generally well organized and includes pseudocode, a notation table, a contiguity proof, solver settings, and model details.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. Equations (3) and (4) contain products such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v), which are fourth-degree, while Equation (2) contains an unlinearized maximum. No auxiliary-variable reformulation is provided, so the stated program cannot directly be given to the claimed Gurobi version and its equivalence to the implemented optimizer cannot be verified.

Pipeline feasibility and costing appear incomplete. Stage contiguity does not force stage indices to respect topological order, and Equation (4) charges only edges from stage j to j+1, omitting reversed or stage-skipping assignments. Moreover, the GPipe objective replaces separate forward and backward bottlenecks with one maximum of their summed costs, and the stated memory constraint does not show the factor for retaining activations from all c micro-batches. These issues can change the selected solution and are material rather than cosmetic.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal solution is unsupported. Appendix E imposes a 60-second limit and permits termination at a 4% MIP gap; the cost model is approximate; and the search restricts pipeline sizes and micro-batch counts to divisors while apparently assigning equal device counts to stages. No achieved solver gaps or exhaustive small-instance comparisons are reported.

The claimed polynomial complexity hides the NP-hard solver behind a constant timeout and omits important dependence on graph edges and pairs of candidate strategies. A fixed timeout bounds runtime but removes any guarantee of obtaining the optimum.

Cost-model validation covers only eight selected solutions rather than the broader candidate set whose ranking determines search quality. Figure 8 is also internally inconsistent: its defined absolute relative error cannot be negative, yet several plotted values are negative.

The headline 3.80× gain comes from one Llama-7B setting. UniAP ties Galvatron on three ENVA models, is slightly worse on ENVB T5-Large, and only ties Megatron on ENVD. Several Alpa and DeepSpeed entries are unavailable or fail, and the Alpa comparison crosses execution frameworks, limiting how broadly the performance advantage can be attributed to the planner.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the central claims: the manuscript provides no code link, complete candidate-strategy construction, explicit DP/TP/FSDP and resharding cost equations, profiling cost, or number of independent trials. Reported optimization time measures UOP but apparently excludes the required profiling stage. Minor wording and typographical issues are secondary; the recommendation is driven by the formulation, optimality, and validation concerns above.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-01rfkvaq/call-12f6e359824242179fe458c65fc71e89/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a consequential practical problem: jointly selecting pipeline, data, tensor, and fully sharded parallelism instead of optimizing inter- and intra-layer choices hierarchically. This unified search perspective is useful and potentially impactful.

The evaluation spans five model families, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge, and four substantially different hardware environments ranging from 8 GPUs to 64 DCUs. Reporting measured throughput, optimization time, uncertainty, scaling results, and an interpretable BERT case study is a meaningful empirical effort.

Several gains are practically significant: on ENVB-8, UniAP improves over the best available baseline by approximately 20% for BERT-Huge, 18% for ViT-Huge, and 37% for Swin-Huge; on ENVC it reports a 3.80x gain over Galvatron for Llama-7B. Results that tie Galvatron on ENVA also usefully show that joint search does not invariably manufacture an advantage.
The exposition is generally organized and readable, with pseudocode, a notation table, hardware/model configurations, a proof of the contiguity constraints, and clearly rendered tables and figures.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: Equations (3) and (4) are not an MIQP as written. Terms such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) contain products of four binary variables. The manuscript neither introduces combined assignment variables nor gives an equivalent linearization; the max operator in Equation (2) also requires an unreported epigraph construction. Thus, the central formulation cannot be reproduced directly as the claimed MIQP.

Material technical issue: Equations (6a)-(6c) enforce contiguity of each stage's subgraph but do not enforce monotonic stage order along graph edges. Even for a chain, a later layer can be assigned to stage 1 and earlier layers to stage 2 while both stage subsets remain contiguous. Edges can likewise skip stage indices. Equation (4) charges only edges from stage j to j+1, so such invalid assignments can receive missing communication costs. No other constraint in the manuscript closes this gap.

The GPipe cost model is only heuristic. Equation (2) replaces the separate forward and backward pipeline bottlenecks with the maximum of their summed stage costs, which is exact only under additional bottleneck assumptions. More seriously, Algorithm 1 constructs memory costs using micro-batch size b=B/c, whereas GPipe's all-forward schedule retains activations for multiple micro-batches when checkpointing is disabled. Equation (5) does not visibly account for this factor, so feasibility may be underestimated.

The repeated claim of finding an “optimal solution” is unsupported by the actual protocol. Gurobi is stopped after 60 seconds and may terminate after 15 seconds at a 4% optimality gap; the cost model itself is approximate; and only a predefined strategy dictionary is explored. The complexity analysis further treats the NP-hard solver call as constant merely because it is time-limited, conflating bounded runtime with exact optimization.

The evaluation does not cleanly isolate the claimed benefit of joint optimization. Figure 6 compares joint search only with inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only restrictions, not with a hierarchical planner using the same cost model, execution engine, strategy set, and compute budget. Comparisons with Alpa cross frameworks, contain several OOM/N/A entries, and do not document matched CPU/thread budgets; the reported 107x search-time result also relies on a timeout lower bound and a proprietary multithreaded solver.

Evidence for the broad performance claims is uneven. UniAP ties Galvatron in three ENVA cases, is slightly worse for T5-Large on ENVB-8, and the 3.80x maximum comes from one Llama configuration. T5 on ENVB is reduced from 24/24 to 16/16 layers, while the DeepSpeed comparison is precluded by the selected batch configuration. These facts do not negate the positive results, but they warrant substantially narrower claims.

Cost-model validation covers only a small set of selected final strategies rather than candidate-space ranking accuracy, which is what determines planner quality. Equation (13) defines a nonnegative absolute relative error, yet Figure 8 plots negative errors. Moreover, the manuscript provides no code link and omits key implementation details such as the missing reformulation, construction of the strategy dictionary, precise profiling procedure, and number of repeated runs. These reproducibility gaps compound the formulation concerns.

The work is primarily a general distributed-training systems contribution rather than a computer-vision method; only two evaluated model families are visual. Overall, the practical idea and promising measurements are worthwhile, but the incomplete central optimization formulation and unsupported optimality guarantee are consequential enough that the current balance favors weak rejection.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a practically important problem: jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies. The unified optimization perspective is clean and potentially useful.

The evaluation covers BERT, T5, ViT, Swin, and Llama across four distinct hardware environments and up to 64 accelerators. UniAP matches the strongest baseline in several cases and reports meaningful gains on others, including 1.18–1.71× on several multi-node experiments and 3.80× for Llama-7B.
The empirical study goes beyond a headline comparison by including optimization time, scalability, restricted-search-space ablations, cost-estimation accuracy, and an interpretable BERT case study.
The paper is generally well organized, with helpful diagrams, pseudocode, notation, hardware descriptions, model configurations, and Gurobi settings.
weaknesses: The central formulation is not an MIQP as written. Equations (3) and (4) multiply placement products such as P_ui P_vi by the already quadratic expression S_u^T R_uv S_v, producing fourth-degree terms. An auxiliary-variable reformulation may be possible, but the required variables and constraints are neither stated nor analyzed; consequently, the presented mathematical program cannot directly support the implementation and complexity claims.

The repeated claim of finding an “optimal” strategy is materially unsupported. Equation (2) approximates GPipe by combining forward and backward costs and implicitly requires their bottleneck stages to coincide; the text justifies this only as occurring “with high probability.” Moreover, Gurobi may stop at a 4% gap after 15 seconds or at a 60-second limit, and optimization occurs over an enumerated strategy dictionary using an estimated cost model. The result is at most an approximate optimum within a restricted modeled space.

Memory feasibility is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b=B/c to CostModeling, while Equation (5) contains no factor accounting for the c forward micro-batches whose activations are retained by the illustrated GPipe schedule; activation checkpointing is explicitly disabled. Unless this residency is incorporated through an unreported mechanism, the model can substantially underestimate memory and return infeasible strategies.

Cost-model validation comprises only eight selected optimal-strategy points, rather than testing prediction and ranking accuracy across the candidate space that drives planner decisions. Figure 8 also plots negative errors despite Equation (13) defining an absolute, nonnegative error. No small-instance exhaustive comparison demonstrates that UniAP actually selects the measured-throughput optimum.

The experiments do not cleanly isolate the benefit over hierarchical AP. Figure 6 compares joint search only with inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only restrictions, not with a controlled hierarchical planner using the same cost model and implementation. Baseline coverage is also uneven: Alpa is unavailable or fails in several cases, the 3.80× result compares only against Galvatron, and the DCU study compares against manual Megatron search and an infeasible ZeRO-3 configuration.

The claimed optimization-time advantage excludes or does not report the required profiling overhead, while repetition counts behind the reported deviations are unspecified. Thus the end-to-end autotuning-cost and statistical claims are difficult to assess fairly.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of source code and insufficient detail about strategy-dictionary construction, graph granularity, profiling sweeps, resharding matrices, and overlap-coefficient estimation. The core contribution is also primarily a general distributed-systems planner; two vision-model evaluations establish applicability but provide limited direct contribution to computer vision or pattern recognition.

strengths: The paper addresses an important systems problem and proposes a useful high-level idea: jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies instead of optimizing these dimensions hierarchically.

The evaluation uses real executions across six model configurations, including ViT-Huge and Swin-Huge, and several substantially different GPU/DCU environments. Reported gains on the bandwidth-constrained ENVB cluster and the 3.80x Llama-7B gain over Galvatron suggest practical potential.

The manuscript includes helpful diagnostics beyond headline throughput: optimization time, a restricted-search ablation, weak-scaling results, a strategy case study, and cost-model error measurements. Solver settings and major model configurations are also documented.

The presentation is generally organized and readable, with a useful notation table and an appendix containing the contiguity proof and experimental details. I reviewed the complete manuscript and appendix :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-29xaqhzv/call-75a005a6888f4e14acb09e8d39ea0afe/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central mathematical formulation is not an MIQP as written. Terms such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v) in Equations (3) and (4) are fourth-degree products of binary variables, while Equation (2) contains an unmodeled maximum. No auxiliary variables or equivalent reformulation are supplied. More seriously, requiring each stage subgraph to be contiguous does not enforce that stage indices follow topological order or prohibit edges that skip stages; Equation (4) charges only edges from stage j to j+1. A reversed stage labeling can therefore omit required communication cost. These are material correctness and reproducibility issues, not presentation refinements.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal strategy is unsupported. Gurobi is stopped after 60 seconds and may terminate after 15 seconds with a relative gap below 4%; the cost model is approximate; and UOP restricts pipeline and microbatch choices to divisors of the GPU count and batch size, apparently with equal-sized stage device groups. No exact enumeration on small instances or achieved MIP-gap results verify optimality.

The cost model needs stronger validation. Equation (2) assumes aligned forward/backward bottlenecks and approximates backward time as twice forward time. Figure 8 evaluates only the ultimately selected strategies—eight points on ENVA/ENVB—rather than showing whether the model ranks the full candidate set correctly. Moreover, Algorithm 1 passes microbatch size B/c into the memory model, but the formulation does not explain how GPipe's c simultaneously retained activation sets are accounted for.

The headline evidence is substantially narrower than the abstract suggests. UniAP ties Galvatron on three ENVA workloads and is slightly slower on ENVB T5; the 3.80x result has only Galvatron as a functioning baseline, while the claimed greater-than-107x planning gain uses an Alpa timeout. The DCU study compares against manual Megatron search and a DeepSpeed configuration that finds no solution. Profiling overhead is excluded, and CPU/thread resources are not controlled despite attributing speed to Gurobi's multithreading.

The experiments do not isolate joint optimization from implementation and cost-model differences. The ablation compares against inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only spaces, but not a hierarchical planner using the same profiler, executor, candidate strategies, and resource budget. Thus the results do not establish that joint MIQP search itself causes the gains.

Originality and scope are not sufficiently established for a 2025 submission. The bibliography contains no work after 2023, while the broad 'first' claim is supported mainly by briefly labeling prior systems hierarchical. Evaluation is limited to Transformer layer chains, homogeneous clusters, and GPipe; the CV contribution is demonstrated only through two vision-transformer workloads.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code and essential implementation details, including the actual polynomial linearization, construction of the strategy dictionary, profiling/warm-up protocol, overlap-coefficient estimation, software versions, and number of independent trials. Reliance on proprietary Gurobi and a platform-specific DCU stack further complicates reproduction.

strengths: Jointly selecting pipeline placement and per-layer DP, TP, and FSDP strategies is a practically important problem. Encoding these decisions in one solver is potentially more flexible than the hierarchical planners discussed by the paper.

The empirical study spans four substantially different environments, including V100, TITAN Xp, A100, and DCU clusters, and evaluates BERT, T5, ViT, Swin, and Llama models. Several measured gains are meaningful: on ENVB-8, UniAP reaches 10.77 versus 8.95/6.27 samples/s for BERT and 45.58 versus 38.74/32.20 for ViT; on ENVC it reports 4.63 versus 1.22 samples/s for Llama-7B.

The paper reports actual execution throughput, optimization time, a restricted-search ablation, weak-scaling results up to 64 devices, cost-estimation measurements, and a topology-aware case study. These provide useful evidence that the implementation can discover effective configurations.

The intended workflow is reasonably clear, and the algorithm, notation table, hardware descriptions, solver settings, and illustrated BERT strategy help explain the system. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-q9oluve2/call-d8be10eb5d084a6d8032cb975f8657e9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central optimization is not an MIQP as written. Equations (3) and (4) contain terms such as P_ui P_vi(S_u^T R_uv S_v), which are degree-four products of decision variables; the nonlinear equality constraints are also not a standard MIQP formulation. No auxiliary variables or exact linearization are provided. Such a reformulation may be possible, but the stated equations do not specify the model allegedly passed to Gurobi, preventing verification of the core method.

The constraints do not enforce pipeline-stage order. Equations (6a-c) make each stage's node set contiguous, but a chain partition whose contiguous blocks receive reversed stage indices remains feasible. Equation (4) charges only edges from stage j to j+1, so reverse-ordered or nonadjacent cross-stage edges are omitted rather than forbidden or costed. The stated program can therefore favor invalid or underestimated placements unless an important unreported constraint exists.

The repeated claim of finding an optimal strategy is unsupported. The appendix imposes a 60-second solver limit and stops after 15 seconds at a relative gap below 4%, so optimality is not generally certified. Moreover, optimization is only over an unexplained strategy dictionary and an approximate cost model. Treating the capped solver call as constant time in Section 3.5 hides the combinatorial solver complexity and is incompatible with the exact-optimality claim.

The GPipe model has consequential apparent inaccuracies. Algorithm 1 passes micro-batch size b=B/c into the cost model, while Equation (5) counts each layer's activation memory once; with checkpointing disabled, GPipe normally retains activations for all c forward micro-batches, so this specification can undercount activation memory by approximately c. The intra-layer-only ablation actually includes a selected strategy that fails with CUDA OOM. Equation (2) also replaces separate forward and backward pipeline bottlenecks with max(fp_i+bp_i), which is exact only under an unverified common-bottleneck assumption.

The evaluation does not isolate the claimed benefit of joint rather than hierarchical optimization. Figure 6 compares the full method only with inter-layer-only and intra-layer-only search, not with a hierarchical planner using the same candidate space, cost model, and execution backend. Comparisons with Galvatron and Alpa simultaneously change planners and other system components and contain many OOM or unavailable entries. The 3.80x headline comes from one Llama/A100 comparison; on ENVA three models tie Galvatron, on ENVB T5 is slightly slower, and on the DCUs UniAP ties Megatron in throughput. These results still show utility, but do not substantiate the main causal claim.

Cost-model validation is too narrow for a search method: Figure 8 evaluates only eight selected winning plans rather than ranking accuracy or regret over candidate strategies, and its negative plotted values contradict the nonnegative absolute-error definition in Equation (13). Profiling time is excluded because the timing covers only UOP, while profiling scope, strategy-dictionary construction, resharding details, solver thread allocation, independent-run counts, and the meaning of the error bars are insufficiently reported. No UniAP code release is identified, and reproduction additionally requires commercial Gurobi.

The demonstrated scope is limited to homogeneous clusters and Transformer models, with only ViT and Swin directly representing computer vision. Scaling experiments increase global batch size with device count and therefore establish weak scaling rather than general parallel efficiency. There is also no loss, gradient-equivalence, or convergence check for the composed parallel execution. Typos and small plots are secondary presentation refinements and do not determine the rating; the recommendation is driven by the formulation and evidence gaps above.

strengths: The problem is important: automatically selecting PP, DP, TP, and FSDP jointly could substantially reduce expert effort and improve distributed-training portability.

The empirical scope is appreciable, covering NVIDIA and non-NVIDIA hardware, 8–64 accelerators, and language and vision Transformers. On ENVB-8, UniAP improves over the best available baseline by about 20% for BERT, 18% for ViT, and 37% for Swin; the reported Llama-7B gain on ENVC is 3.80×.

The restricted-search ablation supports the practical value of combining inter- and intra-layer strategies in the tested settings. The scalability experiments, cost-estimation study, and BERT case study provide useful complementary evidence.

The manuscript is generally readable and supplies notation, pseudocode, hardware and batch configurations, solver settings, and an appendix proof. This assessment includes the complete manuscript and appendix. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-1v9enie6/call-5011e5645b6140ffa8ed88745d99d64f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central optimization is not an MIQP as written. Equations 3–4 multiply placement variables by the already-bilinear term S_u^T R_uv S_v, producing fourth-degree expressions; the max operator in Equation 2 also lacks an explicit reformulation. No auxiliary-variable construction or equivalent executable formulation is provided, so the principal technical contribution cannot be verified or reproduced from the manuscript.

The formulation appears to omit a necessary stage-order constraint. Equations 6a–6c ensure that each stage's node set is contiguous, but do not require graph edges to progress from lower to higher stage indices. Equation 4 charges only edges from stage j to j+1, so reversed or nonconsecutive cross-stage assignments can be feasible while their communication is unaccounted for.

Claims of finding an optimal solution are contradicted by the implementation: each solve is limited to 60 seconds and may terminate after 15 seconds with a 4% MIP gap or after 5 seconds based on a bound. Moreover, optimization uses an approximate cost model. Treating the solver time limit as a constant in Section 3.5 does not establish the stated polynomial complexity or exact optimality of an NP-hard MIQP.

The cost-model validation is insufficient to establish correct plan selection. Figure 8 evaluates only the selected plans in two environments, rather than prediction or ranking accuracy across candidate plans. It also plots negative errors even though Equation 13 defines an absolute, necessarily nonnegative error. No optimality regret against exhaustive measurements is reported.

The comparative evidence is uneven. Several baseline entries are OOM, unavailable, or censored at 40 minutes; the 3.80× headline throughput gain comes from one Llama configuration, while several ENVA results tie Galvatron. Alpa also uses a different framework, and the search-time advantage is explicitly confounded by multithreaded Gurobi versus single-threaded baseline algorithms. Profiling cost and computational resources used during search are not included.

The categorical novelty argument is not adequately established: hierarchical optimization is asserted to be suboptimal without showing that the cited decompositions necessarily exclude the global optimum under matched search spaces. The related-work and baseline set also stop largely at 2022–2023 despite the 2025 manuscript date.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of a code link, the missing executable reformulation, an incompletely specified strategy dictionary and profiling procedure, unspecified software versions and meanings of the reported ± values, and dependence on proprietary Gurobi. CVPR relevance is also indirect: only ViT and Swin are vision models, and the contribution is principally a distributed-systems planner. Together, the core correctness and support gaps outweigh the promising empirical idea.
